hub.purpose: Explain how your company earns revenue, evaluate a growth opportunity, and use financial comparisons to recommend its next move.
hub.centralQuestion: Should this company make the proposed change, and under what conditions?

stages.label: Stage 1
stages.title: Choose a company and decision
stages.work: Complete Start: company, ticker, a short company snapshot, one FactSet learning and feature used, and one tentative decision.
stages.submit: Upload the continuing workbook with Start complete.
stages.grade: Company and snapshot 2; specific FactSet learning 1; a plausible tentative decision 2.

stages.label: Stage 2
stages.title: Follow the Dollar—Find the Next Dollar
stages.work: Trace the company’s current revenue engine, explain recent sales, and develop one evidence-supported revenue opportunity that you can evaluate financially in Milestone 3.
stages.submit: Submit one completed .xlsx workbook with all three tabs. Use your approved project company. No separate report, slide deck, peer-ratio analysis, or full valuation is required for Milestone 2.
stages.grade: Revenue engine 2; history and drivers 2; growth opportunity and estimate 2; feasibility, challenge, and revision 2.
stages.hours: About 3–4 focused hours including class work. Bring your company’s latest annual filing or annual report and access to FactSet if available.

stages.label: Stage 3
stages.title: Compare, Evaluate, and Recommend
stages.work: Evaluate how effectively your company turns revenue into financial performance. Compare two defensible peers, use a brief P/E estimate for market context, and revise your growth recommendation.
stages.submit: Submit one completed .xlsx workbook with Recommendation, Company ratios, Peer comparison, and P-E check complete. Keep the same approved company and bring forward the chosen Milestone 2 opportunity. No separate report or full valuation model is required.
stages.grade: Peer selection and inputs 3; ratios and interpretation 3; P/E check 2; recommendation and revision 4.
stages.hours: About 4–5 focused hours, including class work.

stages.label: Stage 4
stages.title: Recommend and present
stages.dateLabel: PowerPoint: November 30 at 12:30 p.m. ET; presentations: November 30–December 9
stages.work: Use six core slides to explain your decision, evidence, numbers, risks, and next step. Put supporting calculations and sources in an optional appendix.
stages.submit: Upload one editable PowerPoint, then present that file live. Up to 7 minutes presenting and 3 minutes answering questions.
stages.hours: About 3–4 focused hours to prepare and rehearse.

feedback.revision: Revise the existing Stage 3 Canvas submission within seven calendar days of written feedback. The higher score replaces the original. If feedback arrives November 11, the revision window ends November 18. No separate revision file or assignment is required.
feedback.support: Use the Milestone 2 guide and the Follow the Dollar workbook. Milestone 3 preparation will focus on consistent ratio definitions, peer selection, and a brief P/E check.
feedback.finalModel: Use the most recent submitted workbook in your final slides and identify the supporting sheet and cells for financial results.

policies.individualWork: Research, assumptions, formulas, writing, and presentation are individual work. You must explain the submitted analysis yourself.
policies.stageOne: Stage 1 is exploration. Use web research and/or AI plus FactSet. Name one FactSet learning and the feature used. Formal citations and proof are not required until Stage 2. The decision may change as the evidence develops.
policies.sources: Use credible company filings, annual reports, or FactSet reports to support company facts and historical figures. Name the relevant filing or report and useful page, section, or link in your written responses. Clearly label calculations, assumptions, and interpretations. AI output is not financial evidence.
policies.factSetPermission: Students and the instructor may use FactSet evidence in BUS311 course deliverables. Raw exports and screenshots remain in approved course-restricted systems and are not committed publicly or uploaded to public AI tools.
policies.challenge: Use a partner or self-review to challenge the Milestone 2 opportunity. Record the concern and response in Next dollar. Milestone 3 includes a financial challenge and revision. AI may assist the challenge but is never evidence.
policies.aiPrivacy: Give public AI tools only a short summary you wrote from public information. Do not upload workbooks, raw FactSet exports or screenshots, personal information, private teaching material, or nonpublic information. If AI is used, name the tool and purpose in the workbook revision response and disclose it briefly in the presentation appendix or source notes.
policies.missingEvidence: Use the required minimum where evidence supports it. If no defensible peer or comparable historical figure exists, state why and discuss an appropriate limitation or proxy with the instructor. Never invent company facts. Label estimated project inputs as assumptions and explain their basis.
policies.lateWork: Milestones remain eligible under the BUS311 syllabus late-work policy. A late milestone delays feedback and can make dependent project work harder; complete missing milestone work before relying on it in a later stage. Documented exceptions follow the applicable college and course process.
policies.revision: Milestones 1–3 may each be revised once within seven calendar days of written feedback. Replace the workbook in the original assignment; the higher score replaces the original. For Milestone 2, summarize changes in Next dollar; for Milestone 3, summarize revisions in Recommendation.
policies.finalFileLock: The PowerPoint company-analysis project file is due Monday, Nov. 30, 2026 at 12:30 p.m. ET, when class begins. The submitted .pptx locks at that time for every student regardless of Oral Presentation date. Only instructor-authorized accessibility or file-repair corrections that do not alter the analysis or recommendation are permitted afterward.
policies.absence: Approved documented absences use the next protected slot or instructor-scheduled make-up. The live Oral Presentation, including responses to questions, remains required. Unexcused absences follow the BUS311 late-work policy and still require a make-up Oral Presentation.
policies.submission: Keep submitted Milestone 1 work. Submit the dedicated Follow the Dollar workbook for Milestone 2 and the peer-comparison workbook for Milestone 3. The final submission remains one editable PowerPoint and a live presentation.

requirements: Use three comparable company fiscal years and the latest reasonably comparable completed year for each peer. Show exact year ends. milestone2.title: Follow the Dollar—Find the Next Dollar
milestone2.question: How does your company earn revenue today, and what realistic opportunity could generate additional revenue in the future?
milestone2.purpose: Trace the company’s current revenue engine, explain recent sales, and develop one evidence-supported revenue opportunity that you can evaluate financially in Milestone 3.
milestone2.submission: Submit one completed .xlsx workbook with all three tabs. Use your approved project company. No separate report, slide deck, peer-ratio analysis, or full valuation is required for Milestone 2.
milestone2.time: About 3–4 focused hours including class work. Bring your company’s latest annual filing or annual report and access to FactSet if available.
milestone2.sourceStandard: Use credible company filings, annual reports, or FactSet reports to support company facts and historical figures. Name the relevant filing or report and useful page, section, or link in your written responses. Clearly label calculations, assumptions, and interpretations. AI output is not financial evidence.
milestone2.missingData: If comparable history or a revenue breakdown is not disclosed, state the limitation and consult the instructor about an appropriate substitute. Do not invent company facts or a segment split. A forecast assumption is permitted when clearly labeled and explained.
formulaDirections: Revenue history: enter fiscal years in B9:D9 and total revenues in B10:D10, oldest to newest. In C12, calculate middle-year revenue divided by oldest-year revenue minus 1. In D12, calculate latest-year revenue divided by middle-year revenue minus 1. Format both as percentages. If the prior year is zero or unavailable, report n.a. and explain why.

Next dollar: enter additional revenue units in B29 and recognized revenue per unit for the same forecast period in B30, using unscaled currency such as USD rather than USD millions. Enter existing sales displaced in B31 in the same currency. In B32, calculate B29 × B30 − B31 with an Excel formula. Document adoption timing and avoid counting the same revenue twice. A negative result is informative; reconsider the idea rather than forcing a positive number.

classActivity.title: Follow the dollar
classActivity.task: Trace who pays, what they buy, how they buy, how the company charges, and what creates repeat revenue. Start the Follow the dollar tab.

classActivity.title: Find three possible next dollars
classActivity.task: Generate one idea for existing customers, one for new customers, and one new offering or payment model. Identify the payer and willingness to pay for each.

classActivity.title: Choose and estimate
classActivity.task: Choose one idea. Identify the driver, outline the revenue calculation, and flag costs, investment, and potentially displaced sales. Use labeled assumptions when evidence is still needed.

classActivity.title: Defend and revise
classActivity.task: A partner acts as skeptical CFO. Ask why customers would choose this, what assumption is weakest, and how demand could be tested. Self-review is an equivalent option.

classActivity.title: Exit claim
classActivity.task: Write the final revenue claim and identify the most important evidence still needed. Complete historical research, calculations, and revisions after class.

sheets.name: Follow the dollar
sheets.title: Follow the dollar
sheets.intro: Explain how your approved company earns revenue today. Enter responses in the yellow Your response cells.

fields.label: Company and ticker
fields.prompt: Name your approved company and ticker.

fields.label: Student and date
fields.prompt: Enter your name and workbook date.

fields.label: Who pays?
fields.prompt: Identify the paying customer. Distinguish the customer from the end user when they differ.

fields.label: What do they buy?
fields.prompt: Name the major products or services and the customer need they meet.

fields.label: How do they buy?
fields.prompt: Identify the sales/distribution channel and any intermediary.

fields.label: How does the company charge?
fields.prompt: Explain the pricing unit and payment model: unit, subscription, usage, advertising, fee, or another model.

fields.label: What creates repeat revenue?
fields.prompt: Explain repeat purchases, renewals, usage, retention, or why the revenue is mostly one-time.

fields.label: Largest reported revenue source
fields.prompt: Name the largest disclosed segment, product group, or category. Include its amount, fiscal year,. If no breakdown is disclosed, explain the limitation.

fields.label: Follow the dollar summary
fields.prompt: My company earns revenue primarily by selling ___ to ___. Revenue changes mainly when ___ changes.

fields.label: Evidence used
fields.prompt: Name the company filing or report supporting the revenue map. Include a useful page, section, or link. Separate reported facts from your interpretation.

sheets.name: Revenue history
sheets.title: Explain recent revenue
sheets.intro: Use three completed, comparable fiscal years. Yellow cells are inputs. Pale green cells require your Excel formulas.

fields.label: Currency and units
fields.prompt: Use one reporting currency and scale, such as USD millions, for all three revenue amounts.

fields.label: Are these years comparable?
fields.prompt: Explain fiscal-year changes, restatements, acquisitions, divestitures, or reporting changes. Note unavailable comparable figures.

fields.label: What does the trend show?
fields.prompt: Interpret the growth results. Is revenue accelerating, slowing, declining, or uneven? Cite the relevant years.

fields.label: Revenue driver 1
fields.prompt: Name a company-specific driver, explain how it affects sales, and name the supporting company filing or report. Quantify only when the evidence permits.

fields.label: Revenue driver 2
fields.prompt: Name a different driver with supporting company evidence. Distinguish recurring business effects from temporary or acquisition effects.

sheets.name: Next dollar
sheets.title: Find the next dollar
sheets.intro: Generate three ideas, develop one, and revise it after a challenge. Keep reported facts and your assumptions distinct.

fields.label: Idea 1: Existing customers
fields.prompt: What could existing customers buy more often, buy more of, or pay more for? Name the payer and why they would pay.

fields.label: Idea 2: New customers
fields.prompt: Which specific customer group, geography, or channel could the company reach? Explain willingness to pay.

fields.label: Idea 3: New offering or payment model
fields.prompt: What additional product, service, subscription, or licensing arrangement could customers value? Name the payer.

fields.label: Choose one opportunity
fields.prompt: State the chosen idea, why you selected it, the paying customer, and what that customer receives.

fields.label: Is this already happening?
fields.prompt: Label the idea: your proposal, an announced company initiative, or an extension of an existing activity. Cite evidence for any company claim.

fields.label: Why does it fit this company?
fields.prompt: Use at least two pieces of company evidence to explain capabilities, customer relationships, demand, or another relevant advantage. Name the supporting company filing or report.

fields.label: Forecast period and scope
fields.prompt: Define one full year or named 12-month period. Explain whether this is a first-year or steady-state estimate and how adoption timing is handled.

fields.label: What is one revenue unit?
fields.prompt: Define the unit in the calculation below: new customers, subscriptions, transactions, products, or another meaningful unit.

fields.label: Why this quantity?
fields.prompt: Explain the evidence or reasoning behind B29. Label it as an assumption, not a reported company forecast. Name the supporting report where available.

fields.label: Why this revenue per unit?
fields.prompt: Explain the price/spending, annualization, and currency basis for B30. Match B30 to B29 and the period in B23. Name the supporting report where available.

fields.label: Could it replace current sales?
fields.prompt: Explain B31: include sales shifted from existing offerings so the estimate measures net additional revenue. Use 0 only with an explanation.

fields.label: What does the estimate mean?
fields.prompt: Interpret B32 and its uncertainty. Explain why additional revenue may not produce additional profit or cash flow.

fields.label: Costs and investment required
fields.prompt: Identify the main operating costs and upfront investment. Explain the likely cash-flow effect; a full cost forecast is not required.

fields.label: Most important risk
fields.prompt: Name one company-specific demand or execution risk and explain how it could reduce the proposed revenue.

fields.label: How would you test the idea?
fields.prompt: Specify a practical pilot or evidence check, one measurable indicator, and an observable result that would make you reconsider.

fields.label: Skeptical CFO challenge
fields.prompt: Use a partner or self-review: Why would customers choose this? What is the weakest assumption? Record the strongest challenge.

fields.label: Your response and revision
fields.prompt: Explain what you checked and changed, or why you retained the original proposal. State any AI tool and purpose, or no AI used.

fields.label: Your final revenue claim
fields.prompt: Over [period], [company] could generate additional revenue through [opportunity] because [mechanism]. I would monitor [measure] and reconsider if [result].

rubric.title: Explain the current revenue engine
rubric.detail: Identify payer, offering, channel, pricing, and repeat revenue (1); identify the largest disclosed source and connect the map to traceable evidence (1).

rubric.title: Analyze revenue history and drivers
rubric.detail: Use three comparable fiscal years with currency, units, correct growth formulas, and a useful trend interpretation (1); explain two distinct company-specific revenue drivers with evidence (1).

rubric.title: Develop a company-specific opportunity
rubric.detail: Generate three distinct routes with a specific payer and willingness to pay (0.5); choose one, identify its status, and support company fit with two pieces of evidence (0.75); provide a period-consistent revenue calculation and explained assumptions, including displaced sales (0.75).

rubric.title: Evaluate feasibility and revise
rubric.detail: Explain costs/investment and why revenue differs from profit/cash flow (0.5); identify a material risk and a measurable test with a reconsideration trigger (0.75); record a meaningful challenge, justified response, final claim, and identified supporting evidence (0.75).

checklist: My map explains the paying customer, offering, channel, pricing, and repeat revenue, with a supported largest revenue source or disclosed limitation.
I entered three years of revenue, identified currency/units, calculated growth with Excel formulas, and explained two revenue drivers.
I generated three distinct ideas, selected one, labeled its status, and used two pieces of company evidence to explain its fit.
My revenue estimate uses matching quantity, price, period, and currency units, subtracts displaced revenue, and labels assumptions.
I addressed costs/investment, a material risk, a measurable test, the strongest challenge, and my resulting revision.
I identified the company filings or reports supporting my analysis. I can explain my formulas and final claim. I included an AI-use statement or no-AI statement.

legacyDecisionPaths.title: Growth or efficiency investment
legacyDecisionPaths.question: Should the company fund a specific capacity, technology, or process improvement?
legacyDecisionPaths.method: Incremental after-tax cash flow and NPV versus doing nothing.
legacyDecisionPaths.inputs: Initial equipment and setup cash cost; annual additional sales or cost savings; operating costs; tax; additional working capital; end-of-project recovery. Use a bounded five-year project. Explain any estimated project cost using a public benchmark.
legacyDecisionPaths.boundary: Choose a project with a defensible public cost benchmark. A whole-company acquisition, buyback, debt restructuring, or full enterprise valuation is outside this project.

legacyDecisionPaths.title: Working-capital improvement
legacyDecisionPaths.question: Should the company reduce cash tied up in inventory or receivables without damaging service or sales?
legacyDecisionPaths.method: Incremental cash released, implementation and operating costs, and NPV versus current practice.
legacyDecisionPaths.inputs: For receivables, annual sales / 365 × days reduced; for inventory, annual cost of goods sold / 365 × days reduced. Use one lever. Count the release once, explain the duration, and include restoration if the improvement ends.
legacyDecisionPaths.boundary: Use one cash-conversion lever, with two service or revenue risks. Do not count the same cash release again as operating revenue or recurring savings.

legacyExample.decision: Install order-handling equipment for a five-year project.
drivers: More customer orders support higher sales.
Faster order handling may reduce labor cost per order.
legacyExample.peer: Fictional Dockside Supply sales grew 8% in 2025; Harbor grew 10%. Both use calendar years and the same currency.
legacyExample.claim: If the new equipment reduces handling time without raising errors, Harbor can save $3 million annually for five years. Reject this assumption if the pilot savings fall below the break-even level.
legacyExample.challenge: The vendor saving estimate may overstate achievable labor savings.
legacyExample.verification: Recalculate NPV using $2.2 million annual savings, then compare the required saving with a pilot measurement.
legacyExample.judgment: Recommend a pilot before full commitment. Base NPV is positive but the downside is negative; expand only if observed annualized savings exceed the break-even amount.
legacyExample.source: All company names, historical figures, and assumptions in this example are fictional teaching data. They are not a student company solution.
annotations: Three years and two drivers establish enough context to explain the decision.
The $8 million cost and annual savings are labeled assumptions, not reported company facts.
Annual depreciation is $8 million / 5 years; taxable operating savings are reduced by depreciation.
The model compares incremental cash flow with doing nothing. It discounts cash received later.
The downside and break-even test reveal what evidence would change the recommendation.

fields.prompt: State a measurable result or condition that would make management pause, change, or stop. Label proposed thresholds as assumptions.

fields.label: AI-use statement
fields.prompt: Name any AI tool and its purpose, or write No AI used. Keep the final analysis and judgment your own.

fields.label: Final recommendation
fields.prompt: In about 100–150 words, connect the opportunity, financial strength, constraint, P/E interpretation, and recommended next step. P/E does not establish the value created by the initiative.

sheets.name: Company ratios
sheets.title: Company financial trends
sheets.intro: Enter three completed fiscal years, oldest to newest. Yellow cells are inputs; pale green cells require your formulas. Use the guide for definitions.

fields.label: Company name and ticker
fields.prompt: Use the same approved company as Milestone 2.

fields.label: Currency and scale
fields.prompt: Use one currency and scale for all financial-statement amounts in this sheet, such as USD millions. Per-share P/E inputs use unscaled currency.

fields.label: Interpret the company trend
fields.prompt: Discuss all five ratios across three years. Identify the most important improvement and concern. Explain why higher or lower is useful in this business.

fields.label: Chosen industry ratio
fields.prompt: Name the fifth ratio and its unit: times, percent, or days. Choose inventory turnover, receivables turnover, ROA, or another instructor-approved measure.

fields.label: Fifth-ratio definition
fields.prompt: State numerator, denominator, and any averaging. Use the same definition for all three companies. Format row 31 and peer row 31 to match the chosen unit.

fields.label: Evidence and limitations
fields.prompt: Name the filing/report and useful page, table, or link. Explain period-length differences, restatements, acquisitions, missing inputs, and numerator/denominator definitions.

sheets.name: Peer comparison
sheets.title: Compare two industry peers
sheets.intro: Your company’s latest-year values link from Company ratios. Enter one comparable completed fiscal year for each peer. Pale green cells require formulas.

fields.label: Peer scope
fields.prompt: Name the industry and the two chosen public-company peers. Explain the main basis for comparison.

fields.label: Why Peer 1 fits
fields.prompt: Explain customer/product/business-model overlap and one material difference. Being in the same broad sector is not sufficient.

fields.label: Why Peer 2 fits
fields.prompt: Explain why this is a useful comparator and what limits the comparison.

fields.label: Periods, currency, and definitions
fields.prompt: State year-end differences and any currency translation or definition adjustments. Use consistent units within each ratio. Disclose when periods are not fully comparable.

fields.label: Profitability comparison
fields.prompt: Compare operating margin and the fifth ratio if relevant. Explain the company result versus both peers and the selected-peer median.

fields.label: Efficiency comparison
fields.prompt: Interpret asset turnover and the fifth ratio where appropriate. Relate the results to the proposed growth opportunity.

fields.label: Liquidity and financing comparison
fields.prompt: Interpret current ratio and debt-to-assets. Explain a strength or constraint without assuming that the highest ratio is always best.

fields.label: Chart interpretation
fields.prompt: Explain the current-ratio comparison below in one or two sentences. If using an approved substitute, update the chart and its labels to match.

sheets.name: P-E check
sheets.title: A brief peer-based P/E check
sheets.intro: Use share prices from one common observation date and consistent positive trailing diluted EPS. This is illustrative market context, not an initiative valuation.

fields.label: Common share-price date
fields.prompt: Enter the same observation date for all three companies. Use prices and earnings available as of that date.

fields.label: EPS definition and currency
fields.prompt: Use GAAP diluted EPS for trailing 12 months throughout. Enter unscaled per-share amounts in the same currency as each company’s own price. Do not mix trailing and forward EPS.

fields.label: Why these multiples?
fields.prompt: Explain why growth, margins, risk, or business mix could justify a different multiple for your company. The two-peer median is a selected-peer benchmark, not an industry average.

fields.label: Price and EPS evidence
fields.prompt: Name the price source/date and earnings report or FactSet metric/period. Identify material one-time earnings effects or differences in fiscal periods.

fields.label: Interpret the estimate
fields.prompt: Compare the low/base/high implied prices with the observed company price. Explain the uncertainty. A difference does not automatically prove overvaluation or undervaluation.

fields.label: Nonpositive or unavailable EPS
fields.prompt: If company or peer EPS is zero/negative, mark P/E n.m. and discuss an approved substitute or replacement peer with the instructor. Never turn a negative P/E into a valuation benchmark. Otherwise write Not applicable.

ratioGuidance: Operating margin = operating income / revenue. It shows operating profit per sales dollar. Compare business mix and unusual items before attributing a difference to management quality.

Total asset turnover = revenue / average total assets. Average total assets = (beginning assets + ending assets) / 2. Three flow years therefore require four year-end asset balances. A high turnover may reflect business structure rather than superior performance.
Current ratio = current assets / current liabilities. It indicates short-term balance-sheet coverage, not cash available to spend. Inventory quality, timing, and business model matter.

Debt-to-assets = short- and long-term interest-bearing borrowings / ending total assets. Use borrowings rather than total liabilities. For this exercise exclude lease liabilities, applying that definition consistently to all companies; explain any source-definition difference.

Choose one fifth ratio relevant to the business. Inventory turnover = cost of goods sold / average inventory. Receivables turnover = revenue / average net receivables when credit sales are unavailable, with that proxy disclosed. ROA = net income / average total assets. Other measures require instructor approval. Document the numerator, denominator, averaging, and units.
milestone3.comparability: Use three comparable company fiscal years and the latest reasonably comparable completed year for each peer. Show exact year ends. Use the same accounting/ratio definitions and appropriate average balances. Name the actual selected-peer median, not an industry average. Two peers are a small descriptive sample.
milestone3.industryExceptions: For banks, insurers, REITs, or companies where the default ratios are not meaningful, obtain approval for suitable substitutions before calculation. Keep the five comparison positions, but update labels, input definitions, formulas, and the chart consistently. Do not force an unsuitable metric or invent missing data.
peGuidance: P/E = observed share price / trailing-12-month diluted EPS. Use the same share-price observation date for all three companies and earnings information available on that date. Record each TTM end date. Currency units must match within each price/EPS pair.

Calculate the two peer P/Es. Low = the smaller positive peer P/E; base = MEDIAN of the two positive peer P/Es; high = the larger. With two observations, the median equals their mean. These are illustrative comparison cases, not forecasts or confidence bounds.

Illustrative company value per share = selected peer P/E × company trailing EPS. Percentage difference from observed price = implied price / observed company price − 1. Keep the calculation in unscaled per-share currency, even if statement inputs are in millions.

Both peers must have usable positive P/Es for this two-peer range. A zero/negative EPS makes P/E not meaningful (n.m.). Missing data is unavailable, not zero. Seek an approved alternative when needed and explain the limitation. Do not silently omit a peer or apply a negative multiple.

Explain what the estimate assumes about comparability. Historical earnings, unusual items, different growth prospects, and a small peer sample can change the conclusion. The P/E calculation does not determine the NPV or value created by the proposed growth project.

rubric.title: Peer selection and comparable inputs
rubric.detail: Select and justify two defensible peers, naming limitations (1). Provide three years of company inputs and comparable latest-year peer inputs, with dates, currency/scale, definitions, average-balance inputs, and named evidence (2).

rubric.title: Ratio calculations and interpretation
rubric.detail: Calculate five ratios, company trends, and the selected-peer median correctly (2). Interpret profitability, efficiency, liquidity, financing risk, and the chosen industry measure; use a correctly labeled comparison chart and connect findings to the opportunity (1).

rubric.title: Brief P/E calculation
rubric.detail: Use consistent price dates, EPS basis, periods, currency, and positive-earnings treatment (1). Calculate peer P/Es, the illustrative low/base/high range and percentage differences; interpret the estimate and its limitations (1).

rubric.title: Recommendation, challenge, and revision
rubric.detail: Connect one financial strength and one constraint to the proposal (1). Justify a specific pursue, pilot, or strengthen-first recommendation and a resulting change or supported retention of the plan (1). Record a meaningful challenge, independent evidence/recalculation, and reasoned response (1). Specify an owner, timing, success measure, reconsideration trigger, and AI-use statement (1).

checklist: My workbook uses the same company and a clearly stated Milestone 2 opportunity.
My company has three fiscal years, two peers have one comparable fiscal year each, and exact periods, units, and definitions are clear.
I calculated average assets and all five ratios, used one consistent fifth measure, and explained the company trend and peer differences.
My comparison chart links to my calculated results and uses clear labels and units.
My P/E inputs use one share-price date, compatible trailing diluted EPS, appropriate positive-earnings treatment, and correct per-share units.
I interpreted the low/base/high estimate without treating it as proof of mispricing or project value.
My recommendation reflects a financial strength, a constraint, an independently checked challenge, and a measurable next step.
I named supporting filings/reports directly in my responses. There is no separate Sources tab or source-ID entry. I can explain every calculation.
